📌 Toyosa adds BTC alongside USDT for Toyota purchases 

⚠️ Toyosa has introduced Bitcoin as a payment option for Toyota vehicle purchases in Bolivia, expanding its digital-asset checkout service one year after launching USDT payments. Eju TV reported that the company unveiled the Bitcoin service on Sept. 18 at Expocruz 2026 in Santa Cruz, where Toyosa said customers could now choose BTC alongside bolivianos, U.S. dollars and Tether’s USDT when purchasing a Toyota.

📣 BitGo confirmed the arrangement on Sept. 20, saying BitGo Bank & Trust supplied the institutional-grade digital asset wallet infrastructure behind Toyosa’s Bitcoin payment service. Its event calendar places the company at Expocruz from Sept. 18 through Sept. 21, providing separate confirmation of its presence in Santa Cruz during the launch. Toyosa’s Bitcoin service follows a crypto-payment system introduced at Expocruz one year earlier. In September 2025, Toyosa worked with BitGo, Towerbank and Tether to let customers purchase vehicles, parts and services using USDT.

🔔 Toyosa’s existing online payment page still describes the USDT workflow. Customers first obtain a quotation, select a supported blockchain network and scan a QR code from a crypto wallet. The page lists Ethereum and Tron among supported USDT networks and identifies Towerbank as the financial partner and BitGo as the blockchain technology provider. The public page reviewed on Sept. 20 had not yet been updated with a separate Bitcoin checkout guide, even though Toyosa and BitGo had announced that BTC purchases were available. Neither company had publicly disclosed supported Bitcoin wallet types, confirmation requirements, exchange-rate methodology or whether customers face transaction limits.

Speaking at a ceremony on Saturday, Kolivand described the challenges facing rescue teams during the wars, saying search and rescue operations involved extremely difficult conditions and painful moments.

Shabbat Shalom from Galilee, Israel.

The book of Acts closes with the great apostle Paul under house arrest in Rome. There, he called the local Jewish leaders together and delivered a message of profound importance.

He called them his brothers.
He identified himself as one of their people.
He had no accusation to bring against his nation.
And he declared that it was for the hope of Israel that he was bound in chains. (Acts 28:17–20)

Jesus is the hope of Israel.

Faith in Him did not erase the apostles’ identity as members of the nation of Israel. Paul’s own words make that abundantly clear.

Jesus chose to die in our place. The sins of the whole world had to be dealt with, and that is why He came. He willingly laid down His life, declaring:

“No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of Myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. This command I have received from My Father.”

John 10:18 (NKJV)

That is exactly why John the Baptist, himself a Jew, testified:

“The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, ‘Behold! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!’”

John 1:29 (NKJV)

The sin of the world. Every nation. Every one of us.

The involvement of particular Jewish leaders and Roman authorities in His crucifixion does not justify placing collective guilt on the Jewish people. Jesus came from Israel and to Israel, but His sacrifice was for the whole world.

If you insist on limiting the responsibility for His death to Israel, would you also limit the salvation He came to offer to Israel?

You cannot make His death the responsibility of the Jews alone while claiming its saving benefits for everyone else.

Our sins brought Him to the cross. His love led Him to lay down His life. And through faith in Him, people from every nation can receive forgiveness and eternal life.

Finally, consider Paul’s circumstances: addressing a gathering of Jewish leaders while a prisoner in Rome, and eventually facing a martyr’s death. Yet his message was powerful, and the truth he proclaimed was eternal.

Sometimes ministries aren’t big or glamorous. Sometimes their earthly story ends in suffering. Their faithfulness, however, is never measured by the size of their gatherings, their assets, or their exposure. What matters is the message they proclaim.

Unfortunately, many today distort that message to gain exposure, attract larger crowds, and increase their profits. And blaming the Jews for the world’s problems remains a reliable way to attract an audience.

But one day, they will stand before the One to whom the Father has committed all judgment, and they will have to answer.

If your entire “spiritual” message revolves around attacking the nation God called His own, then your problem is with God Himself - with His sovereign calling, His promises, and His choices.

And remember:

“For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.”

Romans 11:29 (NKJV)
